description: §6.1 left-to-right division binding, and how it forces the shape of canonical form.

cases.rationale: §6.1: a/b/c is a·b⁻¹·c⁻¹, NOT a/(b/c) = a·b⁻¹·c. Both h and K acquire negative exponents and sort among themselves bytewise (K 0x4B before h 0x68), so the canonical spelling reorders the input.
An exponent on a divided term multiplies the negative contribution; the canonical rendering carries the sign in the exponent.

§6.1 binds division left-to-right: only K's operator is /, so m^2 stays positive. The decided canonical form makes each term's sign explicit in its exponent, which is what eliminated the historical single-slash ambiguity (AMB-001) — compare parsing.division.001, whose input differs by one operator.
Idempotence: canonical output fed back in must be unchanged. Input updated to the decided canonical form when AMB-001 was resolved.
A negative literal exponent is now the canonical rendering itself. MW/s on input (see parsing.division.009 family) and MW*s^-1 denote one expression and normalize identically.

A negative exponent after / is a double negative — read literally it means MW*s. With slashes now input-only sugar for negation, refusing double negation keeps the sugar unambiguous; this is a typo guard, not a canonicalization need. Only the error code (AMB-013) is still pending.
A pure inverse is directly spellable under the decided canonical form. This closes AMB-004: §8.1's a/b and §8.5's differentiate can always write their result down.
All terms negative: the expression is spellable with no leading 1, and the negative terms still sort among themselves bytewise.
The inverse input form: a leading 1 followed by divided terms is legal input (per the AMB-004 ruling) and normalizes to exponent form. Writers never emit it.

Multi-term inverse input. Normalizes to the same canonical string as parsing.division.008's literal-exponent spelling — one expression, one canonical form, regardless of which input sugar produced it.
